client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed after getting a low grade on my final project. It's like all my self-doubt has come rushing back, and I'm questioning my academic abilities more than ever. I'm not sure if this therapy will actually help me work through these feelings.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling really overwhelmed and that this low grade has triggered a lot of self-doubt about your academic abilities. It’s understandable to feel uncertain about whether therapy can help when you're in such a difficult place. Can you share more about what that self-doubt feels like for you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It feels like this low grade has put a spotlight on all my insecurities. I keep thinking about how I must not be smart enough and that maybe I shouldn't even be in this program. It’s hard to shake off those thoughts because they just keep looping in my head, making me feel even more anxious about my future.
therapist: It sounds like the low grade has really amplified your insecurities, making it hard to see your strengths and potential. It's completely normal to feel anxious about your future when doubts start to creep in. Can you tell me more about those looping thoughts? What do they say to you, and how do they affect your feelings in the moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Those thoughts usually tell me things like "You're going to fail again" or "You don't belong here." They make me feel really anxious and helpless, like I'm just waiting for the next failure to hit me. I know I should probably try to challenge those thoughts, but it's hard because they feel so true in the moment. I'm not sure how to change that.
therapist: It seems like those thoughts are quite powerful for you, making you feel anxious and helpless. It's completely understandable to struggle with challenging them, especially when they feel so real in the moment. What do you think might help you begin to question those thoughts, even just a little? Are there any past experiences where you’ve successfully managed similar feelings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it might help to remind myself of times when I did well, but I struggle to recall those moments when I'm feeling this way. It's almost like my brain just shuts down and focuses on the negative. I know I should be able to challenge those thoughts, but it feels really daunting, like I'm fighting against my own mind.
therapist: It sounds like you're really recognizing the challenge of shifting your focus from the negative to the positive, especially when those thoughts feel overwhelming. It's understandable to feel daunted by the idea of fighting against your own mind. Can we explore some specific moments when you felt proud or accomplished? Finding even small examples might help you create a different narrative when those negative thoughts arise.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I can think of a couple of times, like when I received positive feedback on a presentation last semester. But even then, I downplayed it and thought it was just luck or that the professor was being nice. It’s hard to hold onto those moments when I feel like I keep failing, so I’m not sure how they can really help me push back against those negative thoughts.
therapist: It’s encouraging to hear that you can recall a moment of positive feedback, even if it feels overshadowed by self-doubt. It’s common to downplay our successes, especially when we’re feeling vulnerable. What if we took some time to reflect on what made that presentation successful? Maybe we can find ways to reinforce those positive feelings and remind you that those moments are part of your journey, not just luck.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate you wanting to help me reflect on that moment, but I still feel skeptical about whether it will really make a difference. It feels like I can analyze why I did well, but then I just spiral back into thinking it was a one-time thing. It’s hard to believe that looking back on that success can actually change how I feel about my abilities now.
therapist: I hear you expressing skepticism about whether reflecting on past successes can truly make a difference. It makes sense to feel that way when the negative thoughts feel so strong and persistent. It’s like you’re caught between recognizing a win and the belief that it was just a fluke. What do you think might help you start to create a more balanced view of those moments, so they don't feel so isolated from your overall abilities?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess I could try to write down my successes, but it feels like a challenge because I’m so used to dismissing them. I worry that if I write them down, I’ll just end up feeling even more disappointed when I compare them to my failures. It’s hard to see how that could lead to a more balanced view when the negative feelings are so loud.
therapist: It's great to hear that you're considering writing down your successes, even though it feels challenging. It’s completely understandable to worry about comparing those moments to your failures, especially when the negative feelings are so loud. What if you approached this exercise gently, perhaps starting with just one or two successes? Sometimes, taking small steps can make it feel less daunting and help you slowly build a more balanced perspective without the pressure of comparison. How does that sound to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Starting with just one or two successes does sound a bit more manageable, but I still feel doubtful about whether it’ll really help. I worry that I might just focus on the negatives again once I write them down. It’s frustrating because I want to believe that this could change how I feel, but I’m not sure how to get past that skepticism.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling a lot of doubt and frustration about the idea of focusing on your successes, which is completely valid. It's hard to shift your mindset, especially when the negatives feel so prominent. What if you approached this as an experiment rather than a guarantee? You might discover something new about yourself by simply trying it out, even if it feels uncertain. How do you feel about viewing this as a small step toward finding a bit of balance, rather than a definitive solution?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I can see how approaching it as an experiment could take some pressure off, but I still can't shake the feeling that it might not lead anywhere. It feels risky to open myself up to that kind of vulnerability when I'm already struggling. What if I just end up back where I started, feeling even worse for trying?
therapist: It makes sense to feel hesitant about opening yourself up to vulnerability, especially when you're already struggling. Trying something new can feel risky, and it’s natural to worry about the possibility of feeling worse. What if you allowed yourself to approach this with curiosity rather than pressure? Maybe you could frame it as a chance to learn more about yourself, regardless of the outcome. What do you think about that perspective?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess approaching it with curiosity does sound a little less intimidating than seeing it as a test of my abilities. But I still worry that I won’t learn anything new or that it’ll just reinforce the negative feelings I already have. It feels tough to imagine that this could be a positive experience when I’m so used to focusing on what I perceive as failures.
therapist: I appreciate your willingness to consider approaching this with curiosity. It’s understandable to feel hesitant, especially when you’re used to focusing on perceived failures. What if you allowed yourself to simply explore these thoughts and feelings without the expectation of a specific outcome? Sometimes, just being open to the process can lead to unexpected insights. What do you think that might look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
